children: THE MARKET MAY BE WRONG ABOUT SEPTEMBER: MORGAN STANLEY
The market decided after Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's speech at Jackson Hole last week that the U.S. central bank would most likely begin raising interest rates as soon as September.
However, Morgan Stanley was going against the flow with a research note led by its Chief U.S. Economist Michael Gapen, issued late Friday.

On Monday traders were pricing in a 66% probability for a 25-basis-point rate hike at the September meeting, up from 57% on Friday and 41.4% a week earlier, according to the latest data from CME Group's FedWatch tool.
Gapen points out that the "straight read of Warsh's speech was hawkish," but still the economist wrote, "We are not convinced it means hikes are coming."

With that, Morgan Stanley is maintaining its view for the Fed to keep rates on hold this year "on evidence of disinflation," according to Gapen.  And if the firm is wrong, he writes that the central bank will likely hike by  50 to 75 basis points rather than something more aggressive.

The economist said that yes, Chair Warsh said inflation is the problem and rate hikes are the tool to fix it but he argued that "he is not a traditional Chair and likely didn't intend it as guidance."

Looking ahead to the August reading of the Consumer Price Index (CPI), Gapen is expecting further evidence that disinflation is happening and he sees that as enough to keep the Fed on hold, although he did say that "it is a closer call now."
Gapen wrote that after the speech a September meeting without a hike risks a round of yield-curve steepening, "perhaps even more than was triggered after the July FOMC meeting."
However, he noted that his firm's inflation forecast says "progress is in the pipeline."

The MS forecast for core August CPI inflation is 0.22% month-over-month, which would imply roughly 0.2% for core PCE inflation, according to Gapen, who says he sees "risks to the downside at the moment."

So he says August inflation numbers could lead to improvement in underlying inflation measures.  If the firm's forecast is correct, he writes, this would mean a 6-month annualized 3.02% rate of core PCE inflation for August, versus 3.46% in July.
While this is still elevated, Gapen said that he thinks "that will be enough to convince the majority of the committee to stand pat in September."
